levels.title: Foundations
levels.blurb: Stop dropping material and learn the basic patterns.

levels.title: Club player
levels.blurb: Patterns and plans that win games.

levels.title: Advanced
levels.blurb: Calculation, deep endgames and sharper openings.

skills.title: Mate in one
skills.blurb: Spot the checkmating move.
intro: Checkmate ends the game, so every move you make starts with one question: is there a move that gives mate?
Most beginner games end with a mate in one that one side missed. The habit is to check every forcing move first: every check, then every capture.
ideas: List every check you have. Is any of them mate?
Look at the squares around the enemy king: which are covered, which are blocked by its own pieces?
A queen next to the king, protected by another piece, is the most common mate.

skills.title: Loose pieces
skills.blurb: Win pieces that nothing protects.
intro: A piece that no other piece protects is a loose piece. Loose pieces are free material, for you and for your opponent.
Before every move ask two questions: which of their pieces are unprotected, and which of mine are? Most blunders at club level are loose pieces.
ideas: Count the defenders of every piece before you move.
A move that attacks a loose piece and defends your own is usually best.
Loose pieces on the same line or the same colour are the first to look at.

skills.title: Double check
skills.blurb: Two pieces give check at once.
intro: A double check is a check from two pieces at the same time. The only way to answer it is to move the king, because one move cannot block or capture both checkers.
It usually appears as a discovered check where the piece that moves also gives check.
ideas: Against a double check only the king can move.
Look for a discovered check where the moving piece also attacks the king.
A double check can win even when the king has a safe square, because the next move can be mate.

skills.title: X-ray attacks
skills.blurb: A piece that attacks through another.
intro: An x-ray is an attack through an enemy piece onto what stands behind it. The piece in front cannot move without exposing what is behind, or it can be traded off to open the line.
Rooks, bishops and queens x-ray along their lines. Watch for lines that look blocked but will open after a trade.
ideas: A defended piece in front of a more valuable one is a target.
A trade can open the line to the piece behind.
Ask what happens if the blocking piece disappears.

skills.title: Trapped pieces
skills.blurb: A piece with no safe square.
intro: A piece is trapped when it is attacked and has no square to go to that is safe. Bishops and knights near the edge, and queens that wander too far, are the usual victims.
To trap a piece, attack it and take away its escape squares with other pieces and pawns.
ideas: List every square the piece can move to. Which are attacked?
Edge and corner pieces have fewer escapes.
A pawn move that takes away the last escape square often wins the piece.

skills.title: Mate in two
skills.blurb: Find the forcing first move.
intro: A mate in two needs a first move your opponent cannot meet, followed by mate. The first move is nearly always a check or a threat that leaves only one reply.
Work backwards: picture the final mating position, then look for the move that forces it.
ideas: Try every check first. A check limits your opponent to few replies.
Quiet moves that threaten mate in one can also work.
Check that every defence loses before you play it.

skills.title: Defensive moves
skills.blurb: Find the only move that holds.
intro: Defending is a skill of its own. When your opponent threatens something, the best answer is rarely the first one you see.
These positions ask for the only move that saves the game. Take your time: look at the threat first, then at all the ways to meet it.
ideas: Name the threat in one sentence before you move.
Check, capture and threaten: look at your own forcing moves too.
If every defence loses, look for a counter-attack.

skills.title: Opening tactics
skills.blurb: Tactics that come up in the first ten moves.
intro: Many games are decided in the first ten moves by a tactic that one side missed. Learning to see them early saves a lot of effort.
These positions all arise from the opening. They teach you what to watch for after a developing move.
ideas: Before each opening move ask what it leaves undefended.
The f2 and f7 squares are the weakest early on.
A lead in development makes every tactic stronger.

skills.title: Promotion
skills.blurb: Get a pawn to the last rank.
intro: A pawn that reaches the last rank becomes a queen, usually the strongest idea in an endgame. Plans centre on removing, blocking or out-running the defenders.
Knowing when promotion is possible, and when it only works with a trick like underpromotion, is a core skill.
ideas: Count how many moves the pawn needs and how many the defender needs.
Check promotion with check: it gains time.
Sometimes a knight is better than a queen.

skills.title: Interference
skills.blurb: Put a piece between a defender and what it defends.
intro: Interference means placing a piece on a line between two enemy pieces so that one can no longer protect the other.
The piece you place is often attacked itself, so it must come with a threat.
ideas: Look for two enemy pieces that defend each other along one line.
The blocking piece can be given up if it wins more.
Combine interference with a mate threat.

skills.title: Clearance
skills.blurb: Move a piece out of the way, with tempo.
intro: A clearance move vacates a square or a line for another piece, and it does so with a threat so the opponent has no time to react.
It often prepares a mating attack or a passed pawn push.
ideas: Ask which of your own pieces is in the way.
The clearing move should itself be a check or a capture.
A cleared line is often where a rook or queen lands.

skills.title: Zwischenzug
skills.blurb: An in-between move that changes everything.
intro: A zwischenzug is an unexpected move played before the move everyone expects. It usually makes a threat that must be answered first.
Instead of recapturing right away, check whether a check or a stronger threat comes first.
ideas: Before you recapture, check for in-between checks.
An in-between move can change which recapture is possible.
Look at the opponent's last move: did it leave a piece hanging?

skills.title: Quiet moves
skills.blurb: The strong move that is not a check or capture.
intro: A quiet move makes no capture and no check, but it creates an unstoppable threat. They are harder to spot because we look first at forcing moves.
After you rule out checks and captures, ask which quiet move improves your position with a threat.
ideas: After checks and captures, look at threats.
A quiet move can take away the last escape square.
Look for moves that make two threats at once.

skills.title: Zugzwang
skills.blurb: Whoever has to move loses.
intro: Zugzwang means every legal move makes your position worse. It is most common in endgames, where there are few pieces and few safe moves.
To use it, take away your opponent's spare moves until any move they make is a concession.
ideas: Count the safe moves each side has.
Triangulation loses a move on purpose to hand the turn over.
Opposition in pawn endings is zugzwang.

skills.title: Mate in three
skills.blurb: Calculate a longer forcing line.
intro: A mate in three asks you to calculate a forcing line a few moves deep and make sure every defence fails.
It trains the habit that matters most in real games: calculate before you move.
ideas: Start with checks, then threats.
Write down the replies the opponent can make at each step.
If one defence works, your line is wrong. Look for another.

skills.title: Attacking the king
skills.blurb: Open lines and bring everything.
intro: A king attack works when your pieces outnumber the defenders near the king. It begins by opening lines.
Count attackers and defenders before you sacrifice, and keep the initiative: each move should create a new threat.
ideas: Count your attackers and the defenders around the king.
Open lines with pawn breaks and sacrifices.
Do not slow down: every move needs a threat.

skills.title: Rook endgames
skills.blurb: The most common endgame of all.
intro: Rook endgames arise in about half of all endgames, so every player needs them. The main ideas are rook activity, cutting off the king and the Lucena and Philidor positions.
An active rook is worth more than a pawn. Passive defence usually loses.
ideas: Put the rook behind the passed pawn.
Cut the enemy king off along a file or rank.
Activity matters more than material.

skills.title: Pawn endgames
skills.blurb: Pure calculation, with kings and pawns.
intro: In a pawn endgame there is no room for error. One tempo often decides everything, so you count moves exactly.
The key ideas are the opposition, outside passed pawns, and the square of the pawn.
ideas: Count the moves to promotion for both sides.
An outside passed pawn drags the king away.
Keep the opposition when it matters.

skills.title: Bishop and knight endgames
skills.blurb: Know when each piece is better.
intro: Bishops are better with pawns on both wings and in open positions, knights in closed ones with pawns on one side.
Good and bad bishops, outposts and the right pawn colour decide most of these endings.
ideas: Keep pawns on the colour that the enemy bishop does not control.
A knight needs an outpost.
Activate the king: it is a piece too.

skills.title: Queen endgames
skills.blurb: Perpetual check and passed pawns.
intro: Queen endgames are full of checks. A perpetual check can save a lost game, and a passed pawn supported by the queen can win one.
The king's safety decides them: the side with the safer king usually wins.
ideas: Look for perpetual check when you are worse.
Bring the king close to the pawn.
Do not trade queens into a lost pawn ending.
